title: M35, NGC 2158
caption: The open clusters M35 and NGC 2158, imaged by the Burrell Schmidt telescope at Kitt Peak

recognition.text: Published in the NSF NOIRLab image archive. No published rating.

story: Two star clusters share this approximately true-colour view. The large, scattered one is M35, an open cluster in the constellation Gemini. Toward the lower right, to the south-west, sits NGC 2158, a fainter but more compact neighbour.

M35 holds a couple of hundred stars and lies about 2800 light-years away. At an age of some 110 million years it is a youthful group by stellar standards. Under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye, while NGC 2158 is much harder to pick out through small telescopes.

Here, though, the smaller cluster stands out clearly. The caption credits this to the camera on a research telescope at a good mountain site, which can record faint, closely packed stars that a backyard instrument struggles to separate. An open cluster is a loose family of stars that formed together from one cloud of gas.
scale: M35 is about 2800 light-years away, according to NOIRLab.

understand.summary: The Burrell Schmidt telescope on Kitt Peak recorded this field in visible light with a CCD camera through B, V and R filters, combined into an approximately true-colour picture.
understand.eye: The camera collects far more light than the eye, so the compact NGC 2158, hard to see in small telescopes, shows up clearly here.

explore: Twelve images went into this picture, taken through B, V and R filters in January 1997 with Case Western Reserve University's Burrell Schmidt telescope, part of its Warner and Swasey Observatory on Kitt Peak, near Tucson, Arizona.
alt: A broad scattering of bright stars, with a smaller, denser cluster of faint stars toward the lower right.
